author: BrentDesk Research
headline: The chambers of commerce put entrepreneurship on an industrial agenda because their members are small
deck: An axis on entrepreneurship and innovation reflects who the Federation of Saudi Chambers actually represents.
excerpt: Entrepreneurship and innovation forms one of the Saudi Industry Forum's nine axes, reflecting a membership base dominated by small and medium manufacturers.
content:
Entrepreneurship and innovation is among the nine declared programme axes at the Saudi Industry Forum in Jeddah from 14 September. Its presence on an industrial agenda says something about who convenes the event.

The forum is organised by the Federation of Saudi Chambers through its National Industrial Committee with the Jeddah Chamber. A chamber of commerce represents its members, and the membership of a Saudi chamber is dominated numerically by small and medium enterprises rather than by the large industrial groups that appear in national investment announcements. An agenda shaped by that constituency looks different from one shaped by a ministry or by a giga-project developer.

The distinction matters because the industrial policy conversation in Saudi Arabia is usually conducted at the scale of large projects — a steel mill, a vehicle plant, a petrochemical complex. Those are the investments that move national statistics. But the Kingdom's factory count, which this publication has reported passing 13,600, is composed overwhelmingly of smaller operations, and their constraints are different: access to working capital, industrial land at a scale below what the large estates offer, certification and quality systems needed to sell into larger customers' supply chains, and skilled technical staff they cannot afford to train from scratch.

Those constraints are precisely what determines whether the localisation programme works. A giga-project or an assembly plant can commit to buying domestically, but the parts have to be made by someone, and in most industrial economies that someone is a mid-sized specialist rather than a large conglomerate. This publication has repeatedly noted that the localisation which actually happens clusters around buyers with continuous replacement demand rather than around headline projects — and the suppliers serving that demand are typically small.

The financing question sits underneath. The Saudi Industrial Development Fund lends into this segment, and its terms determine what a mid-sized manufacturer can attempt. A firm considering a capacity expansion or a new product line is weighing a loan against an order book that may not yet exist, which is the same risk allocation problem that appears at much larger scale in the climate finance discussion at Oman Climate Week the same week.

The 2025 edition of this forum launched a Future Industrialists initiative and a Voice of Industrialists platform, both of which are aimed at this constituency rather than at the large groups.

Programme axes and organiser detail are taken from published material; no speakers or session titles had been released for the 2026 edition. Whether the 2026 edition carries that constituency as clearly as the first one did is one of the things worth watching on the floor.
